questions.prompt: Why does a random forest usually generalize better than a single deep decision tree?

options.text: Averaging trees built on resampled data and random features lowers the variance.
It uses fewer features overall, so each tree is simpler and has less noise in it.
Each tree in the forest is grown deeper, so it captures more of the signal.
It fits the training data more exactly than any single tree is ever able to.
options.misconception: A forest usually fits training data slightly less exactly than one unpruned tree. The gain comes from averaging.

questions.explanation: Single deep trees have high variance. Averaging many trees makes their errors less correlated, so the average is more stable.
questions.nextReviewIfRight: Back in your plan when it starts to fade.

questions.prompt: A 95 percent confidence interval (the classical, frequentist kind) for a mean is [4.1, 5.3]. Which statement is correct?

options.text: About 95 percent of the individual observations in this data fall between 4.1 and 5.3.
options.misconception: Confuses an interval for the mean with a range for individual values.

options.text: Given this one interval, the probability is 0.95 that the true mean lies inside it.
options.misconception: Treats the fixed true mean as random; that reading belongs to a Bayesian credible interval.

options.text: Over many repeated studies, about 95 percent of such intervals would contain the true mean.
The sample mean falls between 4.1 and 5.3 with probability 0.95 in this particular study.
options.misconception: The sample mean is a known number that sits at the interval's center.

questions.explanation: The 95 percent describes the long-run behavior of the procedure across repeated samples. Any single interval either contains the true mean or does not.
questions.nextReviewIfRight: Back in your plan when it starts to fade.

questions.prompt: A stakeholder asks: 'So is the effect real or not?' Your interval is [-0.1, 1.2] points. The best answer is:

options.text: No. It is not statistically significant, so we can say there is no effect at all.
options.misconception: Non-significant is not 'no effect'.

options.text: Statistics cannot answer that question, since an interval never says whether an effect is real.
options.misconception: Statistics does answer it, with a range and a recommendation.

options.text: Yes. The effect is 0.5 points, which is our best estimate, so we can treat it as real.
options.misconception: Drops the uncertainty the stakeholder needs.

options.text: Best guess is +0.5 points, but a small loss up to +1.2 also fits. Ship if a wrong call is cheap.

questions.explanation: Translate the interval into the decision's terms: the point estimate, the range, and what the uncertainty means for the choice in front of them.

questions.prompt: A column of ages has 4 percent missing values. The missingness is unrelated to anything else in the data. Which approach keeps the rest of each row and distorts the age distribution least?

options.text: Replace each missing age with 0.
options.misconception: Treats a missing value as a real age of zero, which creates fake infants.

options.text: Replace each missing age with the median age.
Drop the whole age column.
options.misconception: Throws away 96 percent of the real values to handle 4 percent missing.

options.text: Replace each missing age with the maximum age.
options.misconception: Fills with an extreme value and shifts the mean upward.

questions.explanation: With missingness unrelated to other variables and a small share missing, median imputation keeps the rows and barely shifts the center of the distribution. It does shrink the spread slightly, which is the known cost.

questions.prompt: Monthly revenue over three years. Which chart shows the trend best?

options.text: A pie chart with one slice per month.
options.misconception: A pie shows parts of one whole, not change over time.

options.text: A scatter plot of revenue against itself.
options.misconception: Plotting a variable against itself shows a diagonal and nothing else.

options.text: A line chart with months on the x-axis.
A bar chart sorted from highest to lowest month.
options.misconception: Sorting by value destroys the time order, so the trend disappears.

questions.explanation: A single quantity over evenly spaced time is a line chart. The eye reads slope and seasonality directly.

options.text: P(B)
P(A)
options.misconception: Dividing by P(A) cancels the prior and leaves P(B | A), the wrong direction.

options.text: P(A and B)
options.misconception: The numerator already is P(A and B); dividing by it gives 1.
1 - P(B) is the probability of not B and has no place in the rule.

questions.explanation: Bayes' rule divides the joint probability P(B | A) P(A) by the marginal P(B), which normalizes it to a probability of A given B.

questions.prompt: Which plot is the standard first check for whether a linear model's errors have constant variance?

options.text: Correlation matrix of predictors
options.misconception: Shows collinearity among predictors, a different assumption.

options.text: Histogram of the outcome
options.misconception: The outcome's shape is not the error's shape.

options.text: Outcome against time
options.misconception: Useful for autocorrelation in time series, not variance.

options.text: Residuals against fitted values

questions.explanation: A funnel shape in residuals versus fitted values signals non-constant variance (heteroscedasticity). A flat band is what you want.

questions.prompt: Cities with more ice cream sales have more drownings. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: Eating ice cream causes drowning.
options.misconception: Mistakes correlation for causation.

options.text: Hot weather raises both of them.
Drowning causes ice cream sales.
options.misconception: Reverse causation is possible in principle but implausible here.

options.text: It is a coincidence in every city.
options.misconception: A consistent pattern across cities is not a coincidence; it has a cause.

questions.explanation: A confounder (temperature) drives both variables. Conditioning on it removes the association.

questions.prompt: In Bayesian inference, the posterior is proportional to the likelihood times the ______.

options.text: prior
p-value
options.misconception: p-values belong to frequentist testing.

options.text: mean
options.misconception: Sample size enters through the likelihood, not as a separate factor.

options.text: evidence
options.misconception: The evidence divides, it does not multiply.

questions.explanation: Posterior is proportional to likelihood times prior. The evidence (marginal likelihood) is the normalizing constant in the denominator.

questions.prompt: A teammate cannot reproduce your notebook's numbers. The most common cause from this list is:

options.text: pandas rounds decimal numbers differently on other operating systems.
options.misconception: Same version, same arithmetic.

options.text: Their laptop is slower, so long-running cells time out before finishing.
options.misconception: Speed changes time, not results.

options.text: Cells were run out of order, so the results depend on the run history.
Notebooks cannot be shared reliably, so outputs change when they are opened.
options.misconception: Notebooks share fine when they run clean from the top.

questions.explanation: Notebook state is whatever ran last, in whatever order. Restart the kernel and run all cells top to bottom before sharing, and pin package versions.

scenarios.title: Ship the checkout page?
scenarios.context: Your manager shares an A/B test of a new checkout page. The old page converted 4.1% and the new one 4.6%, with 10,000 users in each group. The p-value is 0.08. She wants to ship today.

options.text: The new page raises conversion by 0.5 points, so ship it now.
Inconclusive: the lift may be slightly negative or up to 1 point.
There is a 92 percent chance that the new page is the better one.
The test failed, so the two pages perform about the same.

steps.prompt: Nobody knows yet what a wrong call would cost. What should happen next?

options.text: Ship now, and roll back if conversion drops over the next week.
Keep the old page, close the test and move on to other work.
Rerun the analysis with a one-sided test to get p under 0.05.
Extend the test for a fixed two more weeks, set now, then decide.

steps.prompt: Explain the decision to your manager in one or two lines.
steps.sampleUserAnswer: The lift is 0.5 points but p is 0.08, so I would extend the test before shipping.
steps.modelAnswer: The 0.5 point lift could range from slightly negative to about 1 point. Extend the test, or ship only if a wrong call is cheap.

checkpoints.text: States the estimate and that the range includes zero
Ties the call to the cost of being wrong
